{{Short description|Mathematical construct}}
In [[mathematics]], an '''interval contractor''' (or '''contractor''' for short)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Jaulin|first1=Luc|last2=Kieffer|first2=Michel|last3=Didrit|first3=Olivier|last4=Walter|first4=Eric|
title=Applied Interval Analysis|year=2001|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin|isbn=1-85233-219-0}}
</ref> associated to a set <math>X</math> is  an operator <math>C</math> which associates to a [[hyperrectangle]] <math>[x]</math> in <math>\bold{R}^n</math> another box <math>C([x])</math> of <math>\bold{R}^n</math>  such that the two following properties are always satisfied:

* <math>C([x]) \subset [x]</math> (contractance property)
* <math>C([x]) \cap X = [x] \cap X</math> (completeness property)

A ''contractor associated to a [[constraint algorithm|constraint]]'' (such as an [[equation]] or an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]]) is a 
contractor associated to the set <math>X</math> of all <math>x</math> which satisfy the constraint.  
Contractors make it possible to improve the efficiency of [[branch and bound|branch-and-bound]] algorithms classically used in [[Interval arithmetic|interval analysis]].

==Properties of contractors==

A contractor ''C'' is [[Monotonic function|monotonic]] if we have 
<math>[x] \subset [y] \Rightarrow C([x])\subset C([y])</math>.

It is ''minimal'' if for all boxes [''x''], we have 
<math>C([x]) = [[x]\cap X]</math>,
where [''A''] is the ''interval hull'' of the set ''A'', i.e., the smallest
box enclosing ''A''.

The contractor ''C'' is ''thin'' if for all points ''x'',
<math>C(\{x\}) = \{x\}\cap X</math>
where {''x''} denotes the degenerated box enclosing ''x'' as a single point.

The contractor ''C'' is ''[[idempotent]]'' if for all boxes [''x''], we have
<math>C \circ C([x]) = C([x]).</math>

The contractor ''C'' is ''[[Convergent matrix|convergent]]'' if for all sequences [''x''](''k'') of boxes containing ''x'', we have
<math>[x](k) \rightarrow x \implies C([x](k))\rightarrow \{x\} \cap X.</math>

==Illustration==

Figure 1 represents the set ''X'' painted grey and some boxes, some of them degenerated (i.e., they correspond to singletons). Figure 2 represents these boxes 
after [[contraction mapping|contraction]]. Note that no point of ''X'' has been removed by the contractor. The contractor
is minimal for the cyan box but is pessimistic for the green one. All degenerated blue boxes are contracted to
the [[empty set|empty]] box. The magenta box and the red box cannot be contracted.

[[File:Wiki contractor before.jpg|thumb|Figure 1: Boxes before contraction]]
[[File:Wiki contractor after.jpg|thumb|Figure 2: Boxes after contraction]]

==Contractor algebra==

Some operations can be performed on contractors to build more complex contractors.
<ref>
{{cite journal|last1=Chabert|first1=G.|last2=Jaulin|first2=L.|
title=Contractor programming|
journal=Artificial Intelligence|
year=2009|volume=173|issue=11|
url=http://www.ensta-bretagne.fr/jaulin/paper_chabert_quimper.pdf|doi=10.1016/j.artint.2009.03.002|pages=1079–1100|doi-access=free}}
</ref>
The [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]], the [[union (set theory)|union]], the [[Composition algebra|composition]] and the repetition are defined as follows.

: <math>(C_1 \cap C_2)([x]) = C_1([x]) \cap C_2([x])</math>

: <math>(C_1 \cup C_2) ([x]) = [C_1([x]) \cup C_2([x])]</math>

: <math>(C_1 \circ C_2) ([x]) = C_1( C_2([x]) )</math>

: <math>C^\infty([x]) = C \circ C \circ C \circ \cdots ([x])</math>

== Building contractors ==

There exist different ways to build contractors associated to equations and inequalities, say, ''f''(''x'') in [''y''].
Most of them are based on interval arithmetic.
One of the most efficient and most simple is the ''forward/backward contractor'' (also called as HC4-revise).<ref>{{cite book|last1=Messine|first1=F.|title=Méthode d'optimisation globale basée sur l'analyse d'intervalles pour la résolution de problèmes avec contraintes|year=1997|publisher=Thèse de doctorat, Institut National Polytechnique de Toulouse|url=http://messine.perso.enseeiht.fr/PUBLIS/these.ps|archive-date=2012-01-14|access-date=2013-05-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114031521/http://messine.perso.enseeiht.fr/PUBLIS/these.ps|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>
{{cite book|last1=Benhamou|first1=F.|
last2=Goualard|first2=F.|last3=Granvilliers|first3=L.|last4=Puget|first4=J.F.|
title=Revising hull and box consistency|
year=1999|publisher=In Proceedings of the 1999 international conference on Logic programming|
url=https://frederic.goualard.net/publications/revising-hull-and-box-consistency_benhamou_et-al_iclp1999.pdf}}
</ref>

The principle is to evaluate ''f''(''x'') using [[interval arithmetic]] (this is the forward step).
The resulting [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] is intersected with [''y'']. A backward evaluation of ''f''(''x'') is then performed 
in order to contract the intervals for the ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> (this is the backward step). We now illustrate the principle on a simple example.

Consider the constraint
<math>(x_1+x_2)\cdot x_3 \in [1,2].</math>
We can evaluate the function ''f''(''x'') by introducing the two intermediate
[[Dependent and independent variables|variables]] ''a'' and ''b'', as follows

: <math>a = x_1+x_2</math>

: <math>b =a \cdot x_3</math>

The two previous constraints are called ''forward constraints''. We get the ''backward constraints'' 
by taking each forward constraint in the reverse order and isolating each variable on the right hand side.  We get

: <math>x_3 = \frac{b}{a}</math>

: <math>a = \frac{b}{x_3}</math>

: <math>x_1 = a-x_2</math>

: <math>x_2 = a-x_1</math>

The resulting forward/backward contractor 
<math> C([x_1],[x_2],[x_3])</math>
is obtained by evaluating the forward and the backward constraints using [[interval arithmetic|interval analysis]].

: <math>[a] = [x_1]+[x_2]</math>

: <math>[b] = [a] \cdot [x_3]</math>

: <math>[b] = [b] \cap [1,2]</math>

: <math>[x_3] = [x_3]\ \cap \ \frac{[b]}{[a]}</math>

: <math>[a] = [a] \cap \frac{[b]}{[x_3]}</math>

: <math>[x_1] = [x_1]\ \cap \ \ [a]-[x_2]</math>

: <math>[x_2] = [x_2]\ \cap \ \ [a]-[x_1]</math>
